documents: Abasaghi et al. 2023, Geological Journal 58:170-194, published paper (PDF)

entry.evidence: Despite the previous arguments, other vital issues related to these deposits have not yet been fully resolved, especially in the palaeoenvironmental and sedimentological aspects.

steps.action: States the unresolved palaeoenvironmental and sedimentological questions and four aims: petrography, mineralogy and geochemistry, lateritization factors, parental affinity, and palaeoclimate and palaeogeography.
steps.quote: other vital issues related to these deposits have not yet been fully resolved, especially in the palaeoenvironmental and sedimentological aspects

steps.action: Selects four Permian-Triassic boundary sections (Ghoznavi, Kalateh, Shahmirzad, Ruteh), describes their units and samples each unit.
steps.quote: One sample was taken from each unit for further studies (G1-G7).

steps.action: Describes four lithofacies from outcrop and thin sections and identifies mineral phases by XRD, then measures major oxides by XRF.
steps.quote: The XRD results showed that haematite and goethite are the dominant iron-bearing minerals in our study.

steps.action: Plots samples on the Aleva (1994) Fe2O3-Al2O3-SiO2 ternary diagram to classify them as laterite, kaolinitic laterite or bauxitic kaolinite.
steps.quote: was used as a tool for determining the types of

steps.action: Computes correlation coefficients among major oxides (n = 19) to infer element behaviour and host minerals.
steps.quote: the correlation coefficient (r) calculation helped us measure the strength of the relationship between the major oxides (Table 3)

steps.action: Reports trace element and REE concentrations from ICP-MS and their correlations with major oxides.
steps.quote: Laterites showed a higher concentration of trace elements relative to other lithologies.

steps.action: Interprets the oxide and trace element correlations as Si leaching with Fe and Al enrichment, and trace elements as hosted by oxide-bearing minerals (anatase, diaspore, boehmite, clays).
steps.quote: the distribution of these trace elements has mainly controlled by minerals containing these oxides

steps.action: Poses the parent rock question with candidate sources (mafic, intermediate, felsic, carbonate bedrock) to be tested with immobile element proxies.
steps.quote: Given the importance of the parent rock type, several methods have been proposed to address this issue based on the elemental concentration.

steps.action: Takes published discrimination fields and reference compositions (Hayashi Al2O3/TiO2 < 21; Schieber; Schroll & Sauer; UCC, MORB, OIB, PM, limestone) as the expectation for each parent type.
steps.quote: The samples derived from mafic and intermediate parent material show higher TiO2 and lower SiO2

steps.action: Compares sample Al2O3/TiO2 and Cr-Ni values with the reference fields; most samples fall in the mafic-intermediate or granite-to-basalt areas.
steps.quote: confirms that most samples lie in the mafic and intermediate area (Figure 7a)

steps.action: Checks provenance with further independent proxies: Eu/Eu* relative to UCC, Sm/Nd-Eu/Eu* and TiO2/Al2O3-Eu/Eu* diagrams, and UCC-normalized REE patterns.
steps.quote: The evidence demonstrates that the distribution patterns of REEs in our study are more similar to mafic rocks.

steps.action: Excludes the underlying Ruteh limestone as parent rock, using the measured limestone sample's Sm/Nd-Eu/Eu* position and REE pattern.
steps.quote: Data distance from the Ruteh values rules out the parent rock being limestone bedrock.

steps.action: Keeps a dual mafic and intermediate origin: mafic for laterites, intermediate to mafic for kaolinitic laterites and bauxitic kaolinites.
steps.quote: all methods used indicated a dual origin for our lateritic-bauxitic samples, including mafic and intermediate rocks

steps.action: Infers an allochthonous (transported) origin from broken pisolites, lamination, rounded quartz and irregular Al and REE patterns.
steps.quote: Some physical properties of lithologies such as broken pisolites, lamination, and rounded quartz grains demonstrate mechanical transportation.

steps.action: Calculates CIA, CIW and PIA and combines them with clay mineralogy to infer deep to moderate weathering under a warm, humid climate with short dry periods.
steps.quote: indicate the laterites and bauxites underwent deep to moderate chemical weathering

steps.action: Compares the weathering index values with published values from western Alborz (Abedini et al. 2020).
steps.quote: This inference is largely concordant with the values of weathering proxies

steps.action: Uses Ba/Sr ratios as a second leaching-intensity proxy.
steps.quote: the lower Ba/Sr indicates a strongly leached bauxite

steps.action: Builds a palaeogeographic and palaeotectonic scenario from published palaeomagnetism, eustasy and Cimmerian drift work: sea-level fall, exhumation of the Ruteh Formation, equatorial humid belt.
steps.quote: In our scenario, in the Middle Permian, the globally averaged sea level rose during a deglaciation period

steps.action: Assigns the deposits to D'Argenio & Mindszenty's plate-margin geotectonic model (underthrusting plate and transform margins) rather than the plate-interior model.
steps.quote: it could be stated that lateritic-bauxitic deposits formation was related to an underthrusting plate and transform margins

steps.action: Proposes a three-stage depositional model (weathering, migration, emplacement in karstified Ruteh bedrock) with stage-specific mineral formation.
steps.quote: Our studies show that the minerals of these deposits were formed in two ways

steps.action: Infers Eh-pH conditions from Ce anomaly, La/Y and the stability fields of the observed minerals, defining oxidizing and reducing mineral facies.
steps.quote: most samples displayed a negative Ce anomaly, suggesting low Eh, alkaline conditions

steps.action: Keeps a depositional environment in the transitional zone between vadose and phreatic, closer to vadose, rather than a phreatic setting.
steps.quote: the depositional environment of the studied lateritic-bauxitic deposits has been considered in a transitional zone between the boundary of vadose and phreatic zones

steps.action: Concludes on lithology, intermediate to mafic provenance, humid-climate weathering, karst trapping and the geotectonic setting.
steps.quote: The lateritic-bauxitic horizons are the result of the weathering and erosion of intermediate to mafic rocks

tree.answer: Lateritic-bauxitic horizons at the Permian-Triassic boundary in central and eastern Alborz
Minerals and chemistry yes; parent rock, climate and setting no, inferred from traces
Provenance, weathering and palaeoclimate, depositional environment, palaeotectonics
Parent rock (mafic, intermediate, felsic, limestone); vadose vs phreatic; plate-margin vs plate-interior
Published discrimination fields and reference compositions give different expected ratios per parent type
Conditions found in four outcrop sections

tree.answer: Four sections with similar horizons, not treated as formal replicates
Several independent immobile-element proxies agree; limestone control differs
Intermediate to mafic parent kept as best explanation; limestone excluded

end.claim: The Alborz Permian-Triassic lateritic-bauxitic horizons formed by deep to moderate weathering of intermediate to mafic rocks under a humid climate; the products were transported and trapped on karstified Ruteh carbonate in a transitional vadose-phreatic zone.

decisive_move.sentence: Comparing immobile-element ratios of the samples with published discrimination fields and reference compositions (Figures 7-9) is what assigns the intermediate to mafic provenance.

gates.evidence: Sampling was guided by lithology and colour, not by a hypothesis (p. 172). The limestone-parent rival could have been supported by the measured Ruteh limestone sample but was ruled out (p. 185). The mafic and intermediate fields were not set as tests that could fail decisively. Nothing was fixed before the data were seen.

imports.item: Spearman correlation coefficients with significance levels

limits: Single published paper; no review file, so no review sequence. Final-paper moves and triggers are coded from the text alone. Sample sizes are small: 19 geochemical samples, 17 XRD, only one sample at Ruteh, one limestone control, and thin sections not from all samples. No uncertainties are propagated into the indices or ratios, and no age data or isotopes are used. The text gives Eu/Eu* as 0.77-1.49, but Table 2 lists values down to 0.1 (G3); inference: inconsistent reporting. The text reports r without specifying the method, while Table 3 says Spearman. Negative signs appear lost in the PDF text. Sub-claims: weathering intensity, an index-based estimate without stated resolution (best_explanation at most); palaeotectonic setting (underthrusting plate and transform margins), best_explanation built largely on cited syntheses; transitional vadose-phreatic environment, best_explanation; allochthonous origin, best_explanation. Inference: the four sections act as repeated traces but are not analysed as independent replicates.

disagreements.target: Abedini et al. (2018) and Liu et al. (2017): Ruteh shale facies or limestone bedrock as a (co-)source of Permian [...]
disagreements.support: The measured Ruteh limestone sample differs in REE pattern and Sm/Nd-Eu/Eu* from the horizons, so the paper rules out a limestone parent for the studied sections.
disagreements.quote: The REE patterns are different from those of the underlying limestones of the Ruteh Formation

alternatives_considered.alternatives: Limestone bedrock (Ruteh Formation); felsic rocks; shale facies (cited)
alternatives_considered.reason: Immobile element ratios and REE patterns fall in mafic-intermediate fields and away from the Ruteh limestone values
